species.name: Badger
species.hint: Shy and nocturnal, at home in old, undisturbed woodland.
species.note: Badgers live in family groups in underground setts that can be used for generations. They come out at dusk to forage, mostly for earthworms.

species.name: Buff-tailed bumblebee
species.hint: Visits flower meadows in the warmer months.
species.note: Bumblebees can fly in cooler weather than many other bees. Flower-rich meadows and gardens feed them from early spring into autumn.

species.name: House sparrow
species.hint: Likes busy gardens with plenty of insects for its chicks.
species.note: House sparrows have declined sharply in many British towns. Dense shrubs, insects to feed their chicks and safe nesting spots help them come back.

species.name: Hedgehog
species.hint: Needs green, connected gardens in the suburbs.
species.note: Hedgehogs can travel around a mile in a night looking for food. A small gap at the bottom of a garden fence, about 13 cm square, lets them travel between gardens.

species.name: Swift
species.hint: Arrives for the summer and nests in the walls of older buildings.
species.note: Swifts spend almost their whole lives on the wing and nest in small gaps in buildings. Retrofits can seal those gaps, so good retrofits add built-in swift bricks.

species.name: Common frog
species.hint: Look for damp, planted ground in spring.
species.note: Common frogs gather to spawn in shallow water in early spring. Rain gardens, ponds and damp planting give them places to feed and shelter.

species.name: Kingfisher
species.hint: Needs a clean river full of small fish.
species.note: Kingfishers dive from a perch to catch small fish, so they need clear water. They nest in tunnels dug into steep earth riverbanks.

species.name: Otter
species.hint: A sign of a truly clean, wild riverbank.
species.note: Otters almost disappeared from English rivers by the 1970s, poisoned by pesticides and pollution. Cleaner water let them return, and by 2011 they were found in every English county again.

species.name: Skylark
species.hint: Sings high above open farmland with wild margins.
species.note: Skylarks nest on the ground in open fields and sing while hovering high overhead. Wild field margins and meadows give them safe places to raise chicks.

species.name: Barn owl
species.hint: Hunts at dusk over rough, grassy farmland.
species.note: Barn owls hunt voles over rough grassland. Uncut field margins full of small mammals, and nest boxes in barns and trees, help them thrive.

species.name: Stag beetle
species.hint: Its young grow for years in rotting wood.
species.note: Stag beetle larvae spend several years underground feeding on rotting wood before emerging as adults in early summer. Log piles and dead wood left in place give them a home.

species.name: Peregrine falcon
species.hint: Nests high up, on tall buildings that work like cliffs.
species.note: Diving peregrine falcons are among the fastest animals on Earth. Tall buildings work like cliffs for them, and many cities now have nesting pairs.

species.name: White stork
species.hint: Spends the cool months where water stands in the gardens.
species.note: Many of Europe's white storks spend the northern winter in Africa, some of them in the Sahel, feeding in wetlands and watered fields. They also nest on towers and rooftops across North Africa.

species.name: Fennec fox
species.hint: Comes out at dusk where shrubs and trees grow back.
species.note: The fennec is the smallest fox. Its huge ears shed heat and pick up prey moving under the sand, and it is mostly active at night.

species.name: Grey heron
species.hint: Stalks the flooded paddies when there is something to catch.
species.note: Grey herons wait motionless in shallow water and strike at fish and frogs. Flooded rice fields that hold fish feed them well.

species.name: Genji firefly
species.hint: Glows over clean streams on early summer nights.
species.note: The Genji firefly's larvae live in clean, slow streams and feed on water snails, so the adults' early-summer glow is a sign of healthy water.
